speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Eudes Dube (Minister of Veterans Affairs):
subsubtopic: CEREMONY IN REMEMBRANCE OF VE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 25 years ago today the armies of the allied nations in Europe stood at ease after five years of fierce struggle. Victory had been achieved, but at a fearful cost. Nearly 45,000 Canadians had given their lives in the horror-filled days and nights since September, 1939. The end of fighting in Europe, VE Day, was a day of wild exultation, of joy and of thanksgiving, because peace with liberty had been won. We and all coming generations must remember this day some 25 years past. We remember and celebrate not because we seek to glorify war but because we must never forget the horror of war and we must ever be vigilant to maintain peace.
I was vividly impressed this past week by the tremendous sacrifices made by Canadians in this struggle for peace. As hon. members are aware, a Canadian delegation was invited to Holland to participate in ceremonies marking the liberation of their country. One very moving function in which we participated was at the Canadian War Cemetery at Groes-beek. There is the final resting place of more than 2,000 Canadians. This impressive ceremony with our Dutch friends enabled us to pay tribute to those who fell and also to cement our very warm relations with the Dutch people.
This evening on Parliament Hill a very impressive ceremony will be held to mark this twenty-fifth anniversary. Naturally it is our wish that as many Canadians as possible of all ages take part. The event will be telecast on both national networks of the CBC. This ceremony has a dual purpose; it will pay silent tribute to those who made the supreme sacrifice and it will also enshrine the jubilation which was felt 25 years ago when peace was achieved.
I hope the events which will take place in Ottawa this evening will adequately express the gratitude of this nation to those who served. I also hope this ceremony will create in the hearts of all Canadians a firm resolve to move with all humanity toward a world of lasting and universal peace. All members of both Houses, of course, have been invited to attend and I hope that as many as possible will be able to be present.

subsubtopic: CEREMONY IN REMEMBRANCE OF VE DAY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subsubtopic: CEREMONY IN REMEMBRANCE OF VE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we subscribe to the sentiments which have been expressed by the minister. I am sure all Canadians everywhere will join in saying amen to what he has said today.
I was among those who were privileged to be with the minister in the party that went to Holland. It was a very memorable and stirring series of occasions, particularly as we were accompanied by people like General Simonds and other senior retired members of the armed forces who played such a distinguished part in the last war.
[DOT] (11:10 a.m.)
I was personally interested in the visit to Groesbeek since it was my first visit, as it was for other members of the party, in 25 years. It was a particularly memorable and emotional experience when after the completion of the services, Dutch children decorated each of the almost 2,400 graves with a flower. I am sure there were very few people there, even hard-bitten parliamentarians, who had dry eyes when that ceremony was completed. The grass grows green on those graves and the reception of the Canadian people by the people of Holland was very generous and kind. There is still a very warm place in their hearts for the people of Canada and for the soldiers, airmen and sailors who helped in the liberation.
One parting sentiment I should like to express is that one could not see those graves without thinking that the cost of cure is very high. Sometimes the cost of prevention also seems high, but I believe we must all take into account that prevention is cheaper than cure in matters of this kind.

subsubtopic: CEREMONY IN REMEMBRANCE OF VE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a great privilege to speak on behalf of the New Democratic Party and to join with our colleagues in the House in honouring the bravery and the memory of those Canadians who died in the second world war and in celebrating the victory of 25 years ago.
Despite the horrors of war, those who served in the military services will recall the deep friendships that were made among people in the services, the lack of cant, and how the reality of human existence took on a new meaning. I recall that when the war ended on VE day I was in Flensburg on the Danish border. It was not a surprise to us that the war was over. We had anticipated it for quite a while. We won that war not only because we had marshalled brave men but also because the nation at home had marshalled its resources to win the victory.
It has always been a source of regret to me that we have never been able to do the same kind of marshalling of our resources for the purposes of peace, for the purpose of ending poverty, for the purpose of removing injustices from our society, as we have been able to do in war. It seems to me that to truly honour the brave men who gave their lives for peace we should emulate their sacrifice, we should emulate their dedication, and marshall the resources of our nation in order to achieve the victory of humanity that is possible to us. We should not forget that although we cannot do anything for the dead-they are gone-there are still veterans who are living today in dire circumstances, and we should take the noble words that we utter in the House and translate them into something more tangible to show our gratitude to those men who offered their services and their lives to our country.

subsubtopic: CEREMONY IN REMEMBRANCE OF VE DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on this anniversary, I wish to pay a tribute to the veterans who were actively associated with the victory of the Allied forces.
However, if we analyse all the events of the past 25 years, we must unfortunately realize that war has not yet ended and that freedom does not exist everywhere in the world. Indeed, we only have to note what is going on at the present time in Viet Nam, in Cambodia and elsewhere to realize that we have perhaps too much ignored the human factor when real problems have to be solved.
We find among other things that the vanquished in this last war have risen from it with greater success than the victors. We find that affluence deriving from war cannot be achieved in time of peace, and this thought will prevent us from rejoicing at the victory achieved 25 years ago.

speakeroldname: Mr. Steven E. Paproski (Edmonton Centre) moved:
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
That this House, regretting the government's failure to adopt just employment and fiscal policies which would permit our young people to contribute to national productivity and to their own economic independence, thereby encouraging both pride of country and confidence in our institutions, calls upon the government to take immediate and effective steps to help students at all levels to find and develop employment.
He said: I need not remind the House of the seriousness of the situation regarding summer employment for students of post secondary institutions in this country. Only the other day, the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) underscored the seriousness of the situation when he paraded a number of statistics to impress us with the effectiveness of his department in dealing with the problem.
Unfortunately, his statement did not impress, and I can only conclude that again
May 8. 1970	COMMONS
we have evidence of the government shovelling a problem of considerable magnitude under the rug. The end product of government action or lack of action is to be the misery of thousands of young people walking the streets this summer looking in vain for work. I do not expect that the arrogant and contemptuous front row over there will appreciate what this means. The minister said that approximately 641,000 students may be seeking employment this summer-an increase of 60,000 over last year. I have noticed a great tendency on the part of government ministers to deal with statistics which are completely meaningless unless we can relate them to the human factor.
So, let us think about that figure of 641,000 for a moment. It slides off the tongue easily enough, but not so easily when we remind ourselves that this is considerably more people than are to be found in, say, the province of New Brunswick or in Canada's third largest city, Vancouver. Perhaps this fact adds perspective to the problem. I refer to a problem, but that is probably an understatement. This country has a crisis on its hands. Perhaps that is of no great concern to a government whose front row financiers say they can live on $30 a week or who can still sleep at night when there is a national unemployment rate of nearly 7 per cent and three times that rate in many despairing regions of Canada. It may well be that the government would like to see more students adding to the ranks of the unemployed. After all, one must admit that these additions to the statistics would look mighty impressive in the government's campaign against inflation.
But such thoughts might be interpreted as being somewhat facetious, and it is certainly not my intention to make light of such a grave situation as that facing the youth of Canada today. Thousands upon thousands of students throughout this country are already looking for jobs, and thousands upon thousands of them are already finding that there are no jobs. It is a scandalous situation, contributing to the many problems of our present day society and retarding efforts that have been made in recent times to bridge the so-called generation gap.
The greatest failure of this government is lack of imagination. We are running this country as if it were a rummage counter at a church bazaar. Surely, it is time for Canada to wake up and get in the swim. I am concerned about the lack of policy and lack of planning for young people. We would like our
DEBATES	6743
Student Summer Employment young people to take pride in our country, but many are fast losing confidence and becoming disenchanted. In these days of militant protests, I see ahead of us troubles that can be offset only by strong, imaginative steps by this government. There are many young people seeking pegs on which to hang protests, and history has shown that unemployment may be tolerated for a short time by some but it cannot be tolerated for a long time by all.
I find it hard to believe, when I view the government's attitude and action in respect of student employment, that we are indeed living in the year 1970. Nothing has changed over the years. Correction, Mr. Speaker, the number of those students seeking employment has increased substantially and the number of available jobs has decreased because of automation and because of the government's cold, deliberate plan to slow down the economy at the cost of wrecking lives and families. Remember, 641,000 students looking for three months work is the equivalent of another 150,000 persons looking for year round work.
So, we must ask the question: does the government care? I do not seek a smart alec reply from the government benches because we know already that they do not care about the unemployed, the senior citizens on fixed income, and many others who are fast finding that they are the expendable, front line troops in the fight against inflation.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext:
No compassion, no heart.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
I charge that the government does not care. I charge that the government is going to muddle its way through this situation as it did last year and the year before that. Oh, yes, it is all very well for government to trade off its usual, dreary statistics that have the familiar ring of telling only half the story.
The 1969 summer employment survey of post-secondary students, carried out by the Department of Manpower, tells us that 95 per cent of male students and 90 per cent of female students who sought summer employment actually found jobs. But I can eat and digest my hat more easily than I can swallow these statistics. A couple of weeks' work in an amusement park or picking berries is not what I regard as summer employment and I know, after speaking to a goodly number of students, that this was their lot last year.
Many students who managed to find employment last year did not work for as
May 8, 1970

Student Summer Employment long as they would have liked. And when you consider that many are working to try to pay their way through university, I would guess that many had to drop out because they were not able to make enough to pay for their books, let alone their tuition fees. We have heard the minister's grand plan to help find employment for students, but I would say it is still too little and too late. It is time we stopped looking at this as a problem that raises its ugly head every year, and regarded it as a problem we have to live with and to beat. In short, it is about time we engaged in some long-term thinking and planning, not just sticking our fingers in the dyke hoping the tide will go down.
The government should stop looking in its rearview mirror as it tackles this problem because that reflects only past mistakes, past failures. Where, in 1970, is the imagination and the creativity that helped make Canada in the first place? If the government had more initiative and spunk, we might not have to live with such grave issues as this. Why do we still have to accept this summer bottleneck of job seeking and heartache? Has the government given consideration or has it given any direction to the provinces that the trimester system, that is, a year-round operation, might be applied to the universities and schools across Canada?
As far as I know, the trimester system is in operation at two Canadian universities, Simon Fraser University in Burnaby, and Guelph University. Students at Simon Fraser who do not wish to help flood the summer job market have the opportunity to attend university and to work toward a full compliment of credits. It means they can take the fall semester off from their studies to find work, or it means they can continue their studies through the fall and take off in the spring. Certainly, the trimester system has its problems, and most of them because society is not yet geared to accept it. But our society is moving at an incredibly fast rate, and all praise to these universities for helping to set the pace. I only wish we could say the same for the government.
Perhaps we should jump on this trimester bandwagon, particularly today when we are faced with such grave problems in finding jobs for the regular labour force, when many schools and universities are bursting at the seams through spiralling enrollments, and also when more people are moving toward annual holidays at times of the year other than summer. Should not the federal govern-

ment really get its feet wet in dealing with these questions rather than shifting from one foot to the other and saying, "These things are the affairs of the provinces"? That may well be, Mr. Speaker, but I cannot think of a province that would not be grateful for or receptive to positive suggestions that would help overcome some of their problems.
There are many who say that students should receive salaries from the government-you might say a form of guaranteed income. I do not dismiss this idea and I would like to see it explored, but there are other avenues that must also be explored. Should we not be thinking of creating greater government incentives for students hard put to finance their way through university? Where are the scholarship and bursary opportunities that can make the difference between living and plain existing for a good many of the young people who cannot afford to pay their way through university?

To begin with, that is 60,000 more than in 1969. We also learn from government releases and press stories that the federal government is "trying to hold the line" on hiring students to do work for it in 1970, and that probably most provincial governments will be offering fewer jobs to students this year than last year. The situation faced by university students means, for many of them, the difference between continuing their studies and having to drop out of university. This has caused many of them a great deal of frustration. The problem has reached chronic proportions in many parts of the country.
During the last few days and weeks, I have phoned a number of university students across the country and I have discovered, particularly in some of the regionally depressed areas, that students will have a real problem finding jobs this summer. As a matter of fact they will be worse off this year than they were in 1969. In general, Mr. Speaker, I think that the government, and in particular the Department of Manpower, are a bit optimistic when they talk about all students having an opportunity to find work this summer. I do not think this is going to be the case at all.

When this type of financial policy is being pursued by the government there is a general hiring freeze in most industry and business across the nation. The second thing that I want to point out to the minister through you, Mr. Speaker, is the special problems in different areas of the country. Here, I emphasize in particular the Maritimes, rural Quebec and the Prairies. Perhaps the best example is the general picture in the province of Saskatchewan. From talking to university students and personnel in the universities, in Saskatchewan, I know that this year they are having a real problem in finding jobs that will give them enough money to continue studies in the fall. There is a problem here because of the over-all economic situation in the province and because of the slow-down in the agricultural sector which is affecting everyone in the province. We must do something to revitalize the economy of some regional areas if we want to tackle the whole problem of unemployment. If we do not realize this, we are only tinkering with the matter and fooling ourselves. The government must co-ordinate its programs as much as possible with provincial governments in all

Some people have suggested that tobacco farms in Ontario, orchards and places like that, may have extra jobs. Maybe students could be moved from areas without employment into these areas. Of course this would require the co-operation of the federal and provincial governments, but it is one thing that might be given serious consideration.

Another problem which is often overlooked in the whole field of summer employment for students is that women once again are on the short end of the stick. They do not have the same opportunities as men. They cannot drive a truck, work in construction or work in the oil fields. They have a special problem and it must be faced. To substantiate my argument, I should like to quote a paragraph from a report that came from the office of the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) on March 23, 1970. Page 2 of the report reads:
The detailed study indicates a distinct disparity between earnings of male and female students. Male students, for example, earned an average $1,110, while female students earned only $620.
As you can see, that is about half as much as the male students earn on the average for the summer. The report continues:
In consequence males saved more. Male students managed to save an average of $520, while girl students saved $300.
If you were to research the number of males and females who obtained work, I
[Mr. Nystrom.l
think you would find that the men have more chance for jobs than the women. This is only one of the many areas which the government must examine in order to find a solution. As you can see, Mr. Speaker, the problem of student unemployment is chronic. At this time I should like to offer two or three suggestions for long and short term plans to the government. The first thing I should like to suggest, and this does not refer only to the Department of Manpower and Immigration but includes the government in general, is that we undertake a massive construction program this summer to build houses in cities where they are needed, to build schools and hospitals. These things are needed in Canada, and if a massive construction program were initiated it would employ not only the tens of thousands of students needing summer employment, but also unemployed people in the regular work force. These people must be given an opportunity to get into the employment market, to make a few dollars and make a contribution to society. This type of crash program would stimulate the entire economy. It would stimulate cities, would provide better housing, better schools and more hospitals across the country. We must seriously consider this type of project.
So far the government's fight against inflation has produced results which are not what they hoped. It is time the government realized that a new approach is needed. If it does not, more and more people will be unemployed and we will have greater problems involving the students and the regular work force.
Next, I think the government should consider starting some student work study program. Something like this would enable students to do practical work in the community whilst studying in post-secondary institutions. One example is Frontier College, and I want to take a minute to commend the work it has done in the past. I should like also to call upon the government to give Frontier College a grant, extra money to employ students this summer. They could do some social reconstruction work in areas where it is needed. This is one example of the many programs in the whole field of social development that could be pursued by the government. In strict economic terms, I am sure financial minds would say that this is a very important
May 8, 1970	COMMONS
investment. We must have more work study programs like this which would enable students to get a job but not compete with the regular work force.
I have in mind projects like Frontier College, but they could also do work on pollution control, conservation or reforestation. They could work in community plans and organizations. These things would fit in very nicely with the university and post-secondary programs that the students are taking at school, and would employ thousands of people in the summer. Students could be used on many research projects this summer which would not interfere with the regular work force. This is just one of the many things that could and should be done if we are to tackle the student unemployment problem in a positive way.
Because of the general unemployment picture in Canada this year, Mr. Speaker, I suggest that the government begin some kind of student work study program that would put students to work and allow them to make a real contribution to society. Of course, if that were done our programs would have more relevance for students and their opportunities for work.
[DOT] (12:30 p.m.)
I suggest that we can do this. We have the money in this country, the resources and the technology. I do not see why we should not combine all these factors and create a really good program which would benefit not only the students but the people of this country in general. I know if a war broke out tomorrow we would have money for all sorts of new programs. We could afford to put our people in uniform. Why could we not do something similar on a social level, domestically in Canada today? If we are to do good things on a long term basis, we must begin by doing some of them immediately.
In any long term approach, the first thing we must do is reduce the number of students who are seeking jobs at any one particular time. Of course, there is a problem when too many students come on the labour market at one time. We might solve the difficulty by staggering the school year, by asking the universities to set up a trimester system and by making sure the government is involved in student work study programs. If some students teach while others go to university, that would take a great deal of pressure off the labour market. Fewer students on the market would enable those looking for work in the

Student Summer Employment summer to gain employment and conditions would be much easier for the average working man looking for work.
In conjunction with this we must, as part of our long term solution, think of supporting in some way those who go to university or institutions of post secondary education. As a society, we must be willing to provide the amount of money that is required in order that students may be allowed to attend universities. Post secondary education must be available to students regardless of financial or social barriers. I think it is of fundamental importance that we help students. A summer job should not be crucial in a student's decision to continue university or other studies. We must make more money available through loans and bursaries. We must encourage provincial governments to eliminate tuition fees and, eventually, provide living allowances to enable students to pursue the studies they want to pursue.
Those are only some of the things that ought to be done on a long term basis. As more and more students enrol at universities and post secondary educational institutions, the summer employment picture for students will become worse each year. Every year we encounter the same problems and we must work out long term solutions. We must look closely at our priorities in education. We must institute student work study programs which will enable students to become involved in a more meaningful way during summer months with society; their earnings would enable them to continue their university studies, and thus benefit society in general. If we could remove more students from the labour market, those looking for regular jobs would not face so much competition.
Before sitting down, may I say something about the entire unemployment picture that affects young people? The latest statistics relating to unemployment in Canada show that about 40 per cent of the unemployed are under the age of 25. This is something about which we ought to be very much concerned. Many of these young people under 25 who are unemployed are without skills. They need to participate in special training programs, and they must be given opportunities. Not only are people without skills unemployed, but university graduates and teachers are finding great difficulty in obtaining employment this year. Many of these people have families and many of these people need help if they are not to be pushed down into the vicious cycle of poverty.

In this country we promise our young people many things, through television, through the theatre, through magazines and by the example of our way of life. Young people who expect much on stepping out into the world are disappointed when unemployment slaps them in the face, and they find that many of the promises are not fulfilled. It is very important for us to realize the extent of the problem facing young people. As I say, financial considerations should not determine whether young people obtain a university education. Many of them have families; many have great hopes and expectations from Canada, and many of them are threatened with poverty at this time. As a result, many of our young people are becoming frustrated not only with the type of government we have, but with the type of life they can live in this society. Many become dropouts, thus adding to the fund of alienation to be found among young people. This, in turn, contributes to the unrest we have in Canada, the type of unrest evident all across the western world. We must make a real effort to understand our young people, to understand their priorities and their needs. We must communicate with them, because communication is part and parcel of the entire problem in this area that we are discussing. We must try to involve young people in Canadian society and allow them to do many of the things they want to do.
There is too great a tendency in Canada, as there is in the western world and the United States in particular, to just condemn young people for being restless and for participating in demonstrations and protests of one sort and another. We do not try to understand what is actually bothering them and what they want. I think we ought to begin by reorienting ourselves and setting new priorities, and we must do this as soon as possible. We must not adopt the attitude that has been adopted by the vice-president of the United States. He has called student demonstrators "bums". He says, "they are really just bums". That sort of attitude only makes the situation worse.
The entire problem in this field merits the immediate attention of the minister. He will not solve anything over night, especially if he adopts a piecemeal approach. I, therefore, suggest that we must institute a crash program to employ students across the country. We must begin constructing houses, hospitals and schools so that students may be employed for the summer, as well as other working
[Mr. Nystrom.l
people of this country. We must also begin instituting student work study programs which would allow students to contribute to the well-being of society as well as to their own well-being. We must also take into account the many regional problems and difficulties being faced in the Prairies, in Quebec and in the Maritimes, because students in those areas may be unable to find summer employment opportunities. Even if they find jobs, they may be only part time jobs. So, I appeal to the minister to outline to us, when he replies later today, some of the new approaches that will be used in the solution of these problems that affect not only central Canada but all Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank the hon. member who has proposed this motion as it offers us the opportunity to discuss the urgent problem of employment and particularly of student employment.
We hear more and more about the generation gap. Many among us tend to minimize this serious problem. We hear the usual commonplaces: The young have to sow their wild oats. We were like them at their age. It is the teen-age crisis. They will finally settle down and say "enough of this nonsense".
We must admit that a great number of young people today are irresponsible, particularly, and this is paradoxical, in our colleges and universities. There is no use deluding ourselves: the leaders of yesterday as well as those of today have for a great number of years sowed the seed of dissatisfaction and anarchy if not of revolt. If no change is made in the very near future, we shall reap the bitter fruit of such seed.
Mr. Speaker, I may sound pessimistic, but I am sincerely trying to help the government prevent a catastrophe. And I come to the urgent need there is of finding work for thousands of students, not only during the holidays, but particularly when they come on the labour market. If we do not succeed in finding a summer job for one student in ten, what will happen when they all have completed their studies?
The government must therefore make every possible effort to find a reasonable solution
May 8, 1970	COMMONS
and, at this point, I take the liberty of repeating the proposals of the Ralliement creditiste. We recognize the government's willingness to look for solutions, but we also find that such willingness is not enough. Problems are only shifted. Yet, if partisanship could be put aside, the Creditiste solution would perhaps seem like the only cure.
Is it possible that such a wealthy country as Canada has to face such difficulties? Immensely rich, sparsely populated, ready to be developed, what does it lack? Raw materials? One would have to be unaware of the extraordinary wealth of our subsoil, our inexhaustible forests, our most fertile lands and our numerous rivers. Canada is one of the richest, if not the richest country in the world. Is there not enough manpower? That question should be directed to the unemployed and to the people on social welfare. But what is missing then?
As we have been saying over and over again for 35 years, credit should be released in Canada. It is ridiculous to claim that there is no money to develop all materially feasible projects, it would be just as much so to suggest that beavers might stop building dams. Are we then less intelligent than beavers? No. Let us grow up. It is no longer possible to throw dust in the eyes of the people.
I should now like to prove how the people are fooled sometimes. Here is part of a clarificafion made by Mr. Marcel Faribault and published in be Devoir of 7 May, 1970. I quote:
Right after the election-
That is, Quebec's provincial election,
-my comments would not add much to what you have read, seen or heard. I only want to underline that the firm Lafferty-Harwood, so-called investment consultants, by recommending the transfer of securities outside the province, lay itself open to ridicule. When I learned about it on my departure for Europe at Montreal airport on the evening of April 3, I just had time to advise the Montreal Stock market by telegram that this recommendation was stupid, hysterical and partial, and that those responsible should be suspended immediately. On my return last Monday, I was amazed to find that the advice given by those gentlemen had been followed and that the English newspapers had waited almost one month- until the eve of the election-to denounce that operation. This was further evidence that it was or had become a partisan scheming designed to spread confusion, uncertainty and fear among the people. I condemn such methods which I consider dishonest.
But the recommendation was especially stupid, because it only meant the transfer of paper. Well, what is involved? Bank deposits, share and bond certificates. But a bank deposit is the right to sign

I wanted, when I quoted that article, to explain how ridiculous it is to suggest there is a shortage of money. It is as ridiculous as to have Quebecers believe in a flight of capital when tons of paper are transferred to Ontario in Brink's trucks.
We therefore suggest the following solution: We ask the government to authorize the Bank of Canada to grant low interest loans to the companies willing to invest so as to create jobs. Many employers would need additional manpower, but they are unable to pay adequate salaries. Therefore, the government might help them. The capacity for production and consumers' needs exist, the only thing missing is an adequate purchasing power.
Young people are quite willing to work for the welfare of all Canadian citizens by increasing the production, in order to contribute to raise the standard of living. In this way, everyone would enjoy more comfort which is normally what everyone should be entitled to.
Therefore, we are in favour not of austerity, but of generosity. Let the government loosen its purse-strings and promote full employment for all students, without fear of spending too much money.

Mr. Speaker, to my knowledge, highways, buildings, construction and engineering works are not made with money but with raw material, labour and talent. I say to those who maintain the contrary that I have never travelled in my life on a highway paved with money, and have never seen anywhere $10, $20, or $50 bills or even cheques piled up one on top of the other. To my knowledge, a highway is made up of stone, gravel, concrete or asphalt. I do not see any money in there. If we have all those materials and apart from that the necessary labour to build and thousands of unemployed students, what else do we need to carry out those works for the benefit of all Canadians? The only thing lacking is credit.
And that is the reason why we have repeated for years that if money is the only thing needed, why wait longer to issue it?	:

If they finally understand the need of using money properly, putting it at the service of the Citizens instead of putting the citizens at the service of money, we shall in the end solve the numerous problems we have to face every day.
The Ralliement creditiste is always ready to co-operate in any worthy project. Thus the whole population would be grateful to the government and to Parliament if they decided at last to consider in a realistic way the possibility of changing what is really at the base of all our problems, of all our evils, namely the economic system and the financial system, a change we refer to as monetary reform.
Mr. Speaker, I urge the government to consider that aspect of the problem and to stop saying all the time how sorry they are not to be able to do more, because of the lack of money. Credit could be issued on the basis of pur real credit which is worth billions of dollars.
Why not consider seriously making financially possible what can physically be achieved? Then no student would be without work, unemployment would be reduced to the strict minimum, and even Canadians on social welfare could at long last earn their living in dignity. Such an achievement would bring peace to our country, and throughout the world since, through our example, we would encourage other countries to imitate us.

Mr. Speaker, in my turn and, as objectively as possible, I should like to express my views on the topic now being discussed.
Could a more judicious topic have been chosen at this time of the year? Allow me to congratulate those who had the wonderful idea of giving all hon. members the opportunity to discuss this topic, and to invite the government to exert ever greater efforts with a view to allowing the young people to gain their freedom in an important field, that of labour.
Official statistical data prove that a record number of young people are looking for work this summer. We, members of the opposition, see no cause for concern in the figures on student unemployment, in view of the fact that the situation is only temporary.
Unfortunately, I am afraid that this is all the government is doing to solve the problem of our students.
They indulge in futile rhetorics but never manage to bring about any truly efficient results. In a society like ours it is unthinkable

DEBATES	May 8. 1970
that we should deny our youths the opportunity to work and to help in some active way to promote the Canadian community.
The students are, in my opinion, an indispensable factor in the social and economic development of the country. The present tax policy is partly responsible for the difficult circumstances now prevailing in Canada.
The anti-inflationist measures applied by the government are also, to blame, to a certain extent, for the increase in the unemployment rate.
May I be allowed to express my concern about some of the proposed answers. We certainly do appreciate the merits of the publicity campaign aimed at calling the attention of the public to the needs of our students. We welcome the co-operation volunteered by the various intermediary bodies and by private enterprise in order to improve the situation.
We would like however more attention to be paid to the students from the deprived sectors of our population.
Under the present circumstances it would seem to be only fair to give priority to the students whose parents are in the low income bracket. It is always easier for a student coming from an affluent environment to make his way successfully in society.
If the government fails to help the have-nots, nobody will do it. We should have a fairer distribution between the students from the great industrial urban centers and those from the poorer areas. For the latter, the openings are practically nil. We therefore suggest to the government to invest money in pilot projects, in order to allow students to take part in the economic expansion of the community.
In our opinion, there is no other choice for the administration. New jobs must be created, or subsidies to education will have to be increased.
A few years back, a university chancellor stated that education is no longer a luxury. Now, in this era of specialization, it has become a necessity. No young person should be deprived of the sacred right to education, for lack of financial means. Even in the midst of an austerity period, one must remember that the student of today is the pillar of tom-morrow's society.
The climate of insecurity and uncertainty promoted by the present policy can have but deplorable effects on the faith of the young people in the future of this country. If noth-
May 8, 1970	COMMONS
ing succeeds in improving their lot, we will not be able to prevent them from protesting vigorously and denouncing strongly and firmly the failure of our institutions, because we know that they will be right.
By its attitude, arrogant at times, by the enactment of inadequate legislation, is the government trying to induce in some groups of youngsters a reaction which will be reflected in demonstrations and perhaps violence? I hope not!
It is not all to project the image of a just society; this projection must also be translated into facts, by a greater understanding of the problems with which the young generation is concerned.
I will take advantage of this day devoted to the opposition, while this serious subject is examined, to invite all members to co-operate and to offer excellent suggestions both to the responsible minister and to the government. This co-operation is absolutely necessary. In the last resort, the government will have to be forced to act, if that becomes necessary.
Mr. Speaker, I believe that bitter and cutting remarks about some government members, whether justified or not, will not serve the best interests of Canada.
I am not one of those who might wish to limit themselves to such remarks or make charges that are, in the end, useless. I believe rather that the interests of the Canadian people have considerable precedence over those of a political party.
I must recognize the efforts presently made by the government on this matter. It is altogether too easy, for an opposition member or anyone else, to say that a government remains idle. The question is whether it could do better or more.
In the circumstances, with close and genuine co-operation from all hon. members, we shall be able to do better and more.
For instance, I note that the federal government, in the province of Quebec, will create some 2,000 jobs within the armed forces. And it is also said that most of the 150,000 Quebec students will get work this summer.
However, we know that about 60 per cent of them will be unemployed.

Mr. Speaker, the motion introduced by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Pa-proski) affords the House an opportunity to discuss a subject which is of intimate interest to members who have universities and other institutions of higher learning in their constituencies. As the member for Vancouver Quadra it is my honour to represent the University of British Columbia in this House. That university now has 21,000 students in regular courses throughout the wintertime.
It is interesting to note that at present in Canada there are about 294,000 students in regular courses at universities and diploma institutions of higher learning, and an additional 320,000 undertaking part-time courses during winter, leading to degrees or diplomas. If you convert those figures to full-time equivalents, the total number in winter programs, seeking degrees and diplomas, is over 328,000. By 1975 or 1976, this number will have gone up to 632,000, according to a recent projection made by the DBS. In other words, about one-third million students are seeking degrees or diplomas, and by 1975 or 1976 two-thirds million students will be seeking degrees and diplomas in Canadian universities.
For the most part, students do not come from wealthy homes which can support them in university throughout the year. For the most part, students come from workingmen's families, from families that have never had a university student in them previously. It is not a question of a professional father sending his son or daughter to university but a question of the student himself helping to earn the money to pay for fees, board and room, and books. These students are able to do this by working in the summertime, and occasionally by getting a little work during the winter. A recent survey at UBC showed that about 86 per cent of its students worked last summer. From this we can see that there are almost 300,000 students across the country who must have some kind of employment if

they are to continue their university education, and by 1975 or 1976 some 600,000 students will need employment.

Let us take a look at what a student must earn during the summer. I was going to put the figure somewhat lower, at around $1,500, but perhaps the cost of educating daughters is not as great as educating sons. However, I do know from figures provided to me in connection with student loans that the popularity of Canada student loans during the last three years has increased markedly. Let me just quote some round figures. In 1967 there were 64,000 students served through the Canada student loans legislation, in 1968 there were 91,000 and in 1969 there were 110,000. So more and more students have found it necessary to put themselves in hock in order to get themselves through university. I think this condition may indicate two things: first, that the Canada student loans legislation is becoming increasingly popular, and second that perhaps our economy has been on a downward trend and as a result more and more students need loans because of their inability to find employment or other sources of funds. As bleak as the job picture is for the boys, as other speakers have mentioned, it is even blacker for girls. With their pay scales they find it much more difficult to earn even part of the annual cost of their education.
We will have to decide what kind of society we want in Canada. Unless we do, we may find ourselves in the same position as some of the developing countries, in which some of

I see the task force dealing more in areas of physical development.. .possibly because my jobs in the north have been in connection with hydroelectric development and with mineral exploration. I enjoy very much my summers in the bush. My summers are exciting and I feel are a sort of adventure-

Twelve of these were given four days' notice orally and three days' notice in writing, 29 were given three days' notice orally and 15 were given two days' notice orally. I received replies from a number of other departments but I think the trend is clear, namely, that even the govern-

ment was putting the lid on student employment at the end of last August. I think in some agencies or any business we might expect this behaviour, but I do not think a government need be concerned with its example in respect of student employment and employment termination practices.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy to make a few remarks on the motion of my colleague from Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski). Unfortunately, I feel that the thrust of the idea contained in his motion is totally wrong. I am extremely sympathetic to the problem of students. All of us receive many letters from students in our ridings. However, I must be honest and say that I am even more in sympathy with the parents who are unemployed and seeking jobs.
DEBATES	6761
Student Summer Employment I think the problem rests with the educational system. We are tied to an educational structure which was put together 50 or 75 years ago when our society was primarily agricultural. Each spring it was necessary for the students to go out and plant as well as take part in the harvest in the fall. The students now live in a technological, urbanized society. The students basically are pawns in this system. I believe it is time the provincial governments which are charged with the responsibility for education dragged it out of the nineteenth century and brought it forward into the latter part of the twentieth century.
There are many ways in which I feel the problem to which we have been referring today could be tackled. The first would be by making use of the semester system. Our universities should become oriented more toward a semester system in which their students might be taken through to the same degrees in two-thirds of the time. This system is made much greater use of in the United States. For instance, Stanford University functions for 9J months of the year, whereas the bulk of our universities operate at full capacity for seven months. Not only is it apparent that there is an incredible waste in respect of the use of our facilities, but there is also an incredible waste of the time of the students.
Another area to which I think we should be giving serious thought is the implementation and extension of the type of program currently in vogue at the University of Waterloo in their engineering training. This is a program whereby the student spends part of his time receiving theoretical training at university and then goes out on a directly work-related vocation for the balance of the year. Such a program could be adapted to many other programs presently in use at the universities. There is no reason why a similar program should not be adopted for the training of lawyers, dentists, mathematics students as computer specialists, and so on. Such a program could be extended substantially, and I believe our students would benefit proportionately.
With the semester type of program many students would go straight through university rather than taking time off. We should take a second look at the matter of financial assistance for our students. I believe the program should be modified and extended to assist a student in deciding whether he would like to
May 8, 1970

Student Summer Employment stick with his studies for 9J or 10 months and go straight through instead of missing semesters.
I have a non sequitur written down here. I am not quite sure where it should fit in my comments. It is suggested that "the solution to every poor boy's educational program is a rich girl." I do not know whether that applies or not.

wherein the student loans program is inequitable. I made reference to this in making my comments on the Minister of Finance's budget. I think the modifications to be considered should bring that program into line as well.
One of our colleagues referred to the repayment of student loans. He objected to the fact that students were compelled to pay interest on these loans. I believe another area we should give serious thought to is the development of a method whereby there could be a surtax on a graduate's income tax whereby he or she would repay the loan during the working years. This method of repayment would be a more equitable system. It is particularly true in respect of women that when they graduate they find they are saddled with a considerable debt, and then they get married and have a family and the family starts off with the debt. It would seem to me more reasonable if there were a surtax which would be paid on earnings after completion of university.
I believe the guts of the problem is the fact that our educational system has been highly reactionary and has failed to keep in touch with the times. We will have to alter the system and stop throwing all these young people onto the labour market at one time. The system must be modified so that they enter the labour market at different times throughout the year. Some would come out in the winter months, some would come out in the spring, some would come out in the fall, and so on. This could be arranged if students had the option of continuing straight through and taking their education without interruption or missing semesters.
I feel this is really where the problem lies.
It cannot be solved by an attempt to create 

artificial jobs for which our schools have not trained the students. We are faced with the problem of an ever-increasing number of students being brought into the labour market every summer and because of technological advances the number of jobs for which they are suited is diminishing. Mr. Speaker, I want to support my colleague, the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski), in the important discussion this afternoon. I think it is most timely that he has introduced his resolution at this particular period in our parliamentary session, because we are on the eve of the graduation of the class of 1970 across Canada. During the next few weeks thousands of students will be pouring from our institutions of higher learning looking for their place in the sun in the Canadian body politic.
While the hon. member who has presented this resolution this afternoon has concentrated on the employment aspect of the problem, I think there are other matters that we might take into consideration. Useful employment, of course, is basic to any meaningful life and it is inevitable, unfortunately, that at a time when the economy generally is in a state of recession, when unemployment figures are rising-as we have noted in recent debates in this House of Commons-to a level that even in some respects compares with the days of the dirty thirties, our students are caught in the tragedy of unemployment.
The only solution for that difficulty is a more positive program on the part of the government in dealing with the twin curses- they are serious enough to allow me to describe them in those terms-that are tearing at the vitals of the Canadian economic system. I refer to runaway inflation which has not yielded to the blandishments of government policy up to the present time, and the resulting unemployment from the slowdown of the Canadian economy.
Apart from the unemployment problem there are aspects of the difficulty today which have parallels in other periods of Canadian history.
I think the hon. member for Fraser Valley West (Mr. Rose) in his contribution to the discussion this afternoon suggested that this was the first time in Canadian history that we had

a generation emerging from our universities, or involved in higher education, which had no suitable place for it in the scheme of things. That is not quite accurate. I would point out to the hon. member-because those of us whose memory goes back to the 1930's remember that the designation that was used for that generation was almost the same-that in the 1930's they were referred to as the forgotten generation.

I have spotted the hon. member who is now sitting on the opposite side of the House. He says that those who can suggest this afternoon that they were members of the forgotten generation are older than he. I would like to remind the hon. member that age is not a matter of chronological years; it is a matter of vitality of the mind and spirit-and youth is not restricted to chronological years.
We have been disturbed, in addition to this general problem of unemployment, by the events that have been in the headlines in recent days. There is no time to stress them here this afternoon. Unfortunately, in this day and age of instantaneous mass communication the more violent and extreme section of our young population tends to get the headlines, and in recent days practically the whole attention of the mass media and of the press has been concentrated on the tragedy that took place at the Kent state university in Ohio.
Let me go back to other, earlier periods in Canadian history. I recall that there was radicalism in those days as well, a radicalism which was tinged with idealism. I remember, for example, during the dirty thirties, the period of the so-called forgotten generation, that one of the resolutions that emerged from the university campuses of that day was the famous Oxford resolution which went something like this: Under no circumstances will we take up arms for king and country. Most of the young Canadians who were in universities at that time subscribed to that resolution.
A few years later those who had expressed themselves in such idealistic terms became members of the generation that was referred to as the fighting generation. We were recalling the sacrifice, the service and the contribution that that generation of Canadian youth made as we began this session today in our recollections of the twenty-fifth anniversary of VE day. We should not be too pessimistic

Student Summer Employment with respect to the direction that young people are taking at the present time. It was Bernard Shaw, a cynic of another generation, who said that youth is such a wonderful thing that it is a shame to waste it on the young.
I would say that if the government of Canada and all those in authority across the nation- this includes governments at the provincial level as well-ensure the economic climate and environment which provides the opportunities for our younger people, they would respond to the new challenges and the new problems with the same courage and idealism as the generation we have commemorated today.
Education is essential to this process. In the short time at my disposal I will not outline the precise, ideal program that should be followed in the educational process. But we do know today, with the rapid and almost revolutionary changes that are taking place in society, that higher education, continuing education, or adult education-however you wish to describe it-will be of increasing importance. Governments have already responded in substantial measure to the challenge. For example, our National Parliament introduced a program of grants to higher education. We introduced an extensive vocational training program. We have provided a student loans program to make it possible for an increasing number of young Canadians to have the benefit of higher education. There has been a promise for the last seven or eight years on the part of the present government to provide 10,000 scholarships. This promise has not yet been fulfilled by the Liberal administration. Now, when we have a slowdown in the economy and when job opportunities are limited, the government might do well to implement this promise.

I feel that the students themselves, when given an opportunity will provide the kind of leadership that the government or this Parliament has not been able to give in coping with the tremendous problems of the latter half of the twentieth century. When we see the new activism, based on idealism, of Canadian young people, emphasized in programs such as CUSO which has international implications -it is one of the most effective programs conceived and operated by students themselves-and when we see our young people taking the initiative in meeting the challenge of pollution to our environment, these are

I know we have the lunatic fringe of hippies and yippies, the types who get the attention of the mass media because they are controversial. I know there are many psychopaths who might be described as rebels without a cause, or revolutionaries without a goal. These are a small minority. By and large, if the government of Canada will provide the opportunities I am convinced that the majority of Canadian youth will respond and provide the leadership as they have in the past.

Mr. Speaker, I am happy of this opportunity to take part in this debate on the motion put forward by the Progressive Conservative party.
This motion is typically conservative and the Progressive Conservative members knew beforehand that it was useless to discuss it.
If building permits, namely money, did not cost three or four times as much as the building itself, we could hope to be able to provide work for students.
It is only logical to wish to find employment for students, but in order to be able to undertake such works, the municipalities, the federal government or the provincial governments must borrow money at 9J, 10 or 10i per cent and even 15 per cent, when they can barely pay the interest on the debts they already have.
Today, there are thousands of unemployed in Canada, a large number of them in the province of Quebec.
At the same time, many students are coming out of universities and schools, hoping to earn a living, or at least a few cents during the holidays, to pay their studies and fulfil themselves as others have done.
But that has become impossible in our system of running into debts. Indeed, if we want to create jobs, there are all kinds of possibilities. We could give the students countless jobs by undertaking to recondition our rivers and to prevent the pollution of those that are still safe. A project of that kind could give thousands of jobs to the unemployed and the students.
But we do not have that "scrap of paper" which is nothing but an entry in the books, under the name of so and so, and a cheque in

circulation. And when the finance companies receive the cheque, they deduct from the account of one person to add to that of another.
In a proportion of 96 per cent, money is but a mere accounting operation, but the government refuses to assume its responsibilities in that field. In fact, it has given the control of that accounting to private institutions which only allow money to circulate provided it comes back to them, padded by the exorbitant interest rates we know.
That is the main reason why we cannot carry out certain projects in which students could participate during the summer. If we could, we might then take advantage of the students" abilities to involve them in research and in the development of the huge natural resources available in the country and which can only be exploited through hard thinking and initiative.
But we cannot launch such projects because we lack the necessary "scraps of paper". If we really want to take action, we have to borrow these "scraps of paper", we have to get further into debt, we have to impose further taxes on people already overtaxed in every field.
In the field of industry, many students could, during the holidays, help to build new plants or to enlarge existing ones. In the long run, it would provide work for the unemployed.
As for the field of industry, it is still impossible to be concerned about it. Indeed, the federal government now has to deal with a surplus of products worth $34 billion in 1969-70. The government prefers to pay unemployment insurance benefits or welfare allowances. The government does not have the necessary funds to provide employment for students. If students are given jobs, new products will be created. The government does not want that on account of the surplus. This shows the lack of adequate purchasing power. Such purchasing power is not available, because the governments, the ministers, the federal and provincial administrators have not assumed their financial responsibilities.
Technology has invaded all economic fields. Every year thousands of new graduates are unable to find jobs in Canada. About 30 per cent of these graduates, on whom much money was spent, have to leave the country in order to earn a living. Yet we need their science to build and progress.
Unfortunately we lack the necessary funds for settling this problem. Only the Creditistes

are concerned about this problem. They are the only ones to bring up those matters. When it is necessary to solve problems and to bring an end to situations that are as alarming as this one, when thousands of unemployed and of students could be working to accomplish something and to ensure the progress of science, we move backwards or do nothing because we lack scriptural money and we cannot find the way to put some scraps of paper into circulation.

When the building permit, that is the money, costs three times as much as the building itself, it is rather difficult to keep on building. Everything needs to be built. We could build arenas for our young people. Many Canadian cities, especially in the province of Quebec, have none, while they are in need of them. We could have students work on such projects.

In that respect, we are deep in debt, because these works are paid three or four times to finance.
As I said, citizens, members of Parliament, persons responsible, administrators, in other words, all those who have been chosen to administer the country should open their eyes and their ears, and put into effect in Canada a logical economic system based on reality.
