So it is not likely that the people from the universities who flew once with the Prime Minister are apt to fly with him again, unless he puts some meaning into the just society. I raise this point because many hon. members opposite, dear as they
[Mr. Latulippe.)
are to me as friends, are capable of some of the most outlandish gimmicks ever seen on the Canadian political scene.
This remark is not confined to federal members, because their provincial counterparts can come up with some equally outlandish gimmicks. I went through election campaigns in which Diefendollars were talked of around the riding. Now, as one looks back, one sees that that was really the gold age. I wish I had saved them because they are the only currency worth anything today. In a recent provincial election campaign blank notes or partially blank notes were distributed. I point this out to show that the gimmicks of the just society involve utilization of spurious, bogus currency. This partially blank money seems to epitomize the dilemma of those at the university level with regard to the just society. They, in turn, are now part of the blank part of the currency, so to speak.
The students, the veterans, the aged and those least able put up a fight against inflationary pressures are in their turn, the victims of it. Is this the definition of the just society in Canada today? I suggest that it is. I suggest that it is a very apt illustration of the facts. Certain people are asked to bear the brunt of the war against inflation-and students, the people with whom we are particularly concerned, are very much pawns in this war.
The minister, who was a university man, in whose riding a university is a very important part of a person's life and who holds his and other universities dear, has my sympathy. I think it must bother the life out of the minister, who is trying to do a good job for certain people coming under the responsibility of his portfolio, to know that he is associated with this so-called just society. Probably when he takes part later in the debate he will let us know the amount of stress he is under and we will be able to give him a hand and say, "Go back to the cabinet and fight for what you regard as justice for university students," for whom we are looking out this afternoon.
It is probably ironic that the crowd on which the skilful propaganda touch of the Prime Minister had such impact in the last election is probably one of the first to feel the might of his fist when he does not, temporarily at least, need its votes. He is now in a position to exercise power. Is that not ironic? I am sure it must strike you so, Mr. Speaker, and hon. members opposite. Of course,, it is very apparent to members on this side of the House. The young people are the shock-troops
May 8. 1970	COMMONS
in the war to be fought once every four years, yet when the war is over they are left to walk up and down the highways of Canada trying to find jobs that will enable them to attend university in the winter.
I thought the hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) put the problem very Well when he noted that about 641,000 university students are seeking summer employment.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
I am glad to see the hon. member for South Western Nova so thoroughly agreeing with me when I agree with him. He noted a few minutes later in his speech of which I made copious notes that these students will be in competition with 542,000 people, at least, who are already unemployed.
I think the NDP member who spoke also pointed out the dangers and frictions that will arise in trying to thrust one group into competition with the other in obtaining the few jobs that are available. I think that was a useful and good point and reinforced what the hon. member for Edmonton Centre and the hon. member for South Western Nova have been trying to tell the House.
In planning, it is important that we should not emphasize that students should merely take any type of job that comes along because that, sir, would only alienate the people for whom work the year round is important. Students must work merely to tide them over, so that they may attend university. That is the important thing for them. Therefore the objective that the minister, his department and the government must aim at is not the piling up of impressive statistics which might seem to solve the students' problem for a short period of time but not the problem of non-student unemployment, if I might coin that phrase; the objective must be the working toward ends that are in the interests of students while not alienating the two different parts of the labour force.
The hon. member for South Western Nova in calling for a special conference on student unemployment made a very useful contribution to our discussions. I reject the idea of bleeding sections of the economy in the fight against inflation. This is an old-fashioned concept, somewhat older than the Keynesian concept of economics and old when compared with the plight we face in Canada today. When people in future look back at this period of time and find that we sacrificed the old people, the veterans and the students
DEBATES	67S7
Student Summer Employment because of a mistaken notion about the problems of inflation, I think that anyone in Parliament who endorsed the Prime Minister's economic theories will be roundly berated, as well he should be. Those of us who had sense enough to fight those theories and to propose motions such as the the hon. member for Edmonton Centre proposed this afternoon will find themselves among the blessed.
I hope our fight this afternoon is not a futile one. I hope the points we are making will reach the conscience of the government through the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. MacEachen) and that he will tell the government he is not satisfied with its efforts and the direction it is taking in finding jobs for students.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as we meet today more than 600,000 university students either have completed or will shortly complete their studies for the previous school year. More than 90 per cent of them will be looking for employment which will help them finance their next school year. Some time before the end of next month an equal number of students will be finishing high school, technical, vocational school training or CEGEP courses and looking for work. They will find it extremely difficult to find work because according to the latest figures 542,000 adults, or 6.7 per cent of the labour force, are already out of work and are looking for work.
[DOT] (4:00 p.m.)
This is not the first time in modern times that Canada has had unemployment. However, it is certainly the first time since the depression years of the 1930's that we have had unemployment induced and encouraged by government action. To a very large extent our unemployment is caused by the government's deliberate policy to fight inflation. The government adopted this policy on the advice of its economic advisers who obviously have read nothing more recent than the words of President Hoover of the United States when determining how to deal with the economic difficulties of unemployment. They certainly have not heard of John Maynard Keynes. They have not studied the western European countries, none of which has more than 2 per cent unemployment. In Canada 6.7 per cent of the labour force is unemployed. This figure does not take into account the large number of university students now looking for employment.
6768	COMMONS
Student Summer Employment
The figures show that in March 542,000 Canadians were seeking employment. This represents 6.7 per cent of the labour force. The latest breakdown that I have for the provinces indicates that 8.7 per cent of the work force in the province of Quebec is looking for work. Is it any wonder that on April 25 the Parti Quebecois received so many votes? No wonder they got 23 per cent of the total vote and 33 per cent of the Frenchspeaking vote in that province. In the month of January, 14.4 per cent of those looking for work in the age group 14 to 19 years were unemployed. Of those looking for work in the age group 20 to 24 years, 8.1 per cent were unemployed. Those are precisely the people to whom the Parti Quebecois appeals-the new graduates and the university students.
It is precisely because of the short-sighted policies of this government that the Parti Quebecois had such marked success, particularly among the young people, teachers, professors and groups such as social workers. These people saw this happening in the province of Quebec. They are aware of the absolute unconcern of this government about the problem. They know this government is encouraging unemployment in the futile and stupid hope that more unemployment will cool down the so-called inflation and in some magic way stop the rise in prices and create more jobs later.
In addition to our protest the economists in the universities, labour leaders, social workers and the mayors of the major cities of Canada have been protesting. A few weeks ago a delegation representing the Canadian Federation of Mayors and Municipalities met with the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and his cabinet. An article in the Toronto Globe and Mail dated April 21, 1970, and headlined "Unemployment Cripples Cities, Mayors tell PM" reads in part as follows:
A group of Canadian mayors yesterday told Prime Minister Pierre Trudeau that rising unemployment across Canada is crippling growth of their cities.
Mayor Sidney Buckwold of Saskatoon said major urban construction projects "are grinding to a halt" because of unemployment.
I remind the minister that Sidney Buckwold can hardly be called a partisan opponent of the government: he was the Liberal candidate on several occasions.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: He is a fine man.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
He is a fine man; however, the people of Saskatoon in their wisdom did not see fit to elect him even though there

DEBATES	May 8. 1970
were rumours that if he were elected he would be appointed to the cabinet. The article continues:
"Representatives of cities across the nation have said that architects' offices in their areas are just not busy."
Mr. Buckwold said municipal leaders in Canada are deeply concerned about the construction prospects for 1971. "The work is just not building up."
One does not need statistics to know that, Mr. Speaker. Housing starts are down drastically-50 per cent or more. In every Canadian city the starts on large projects such as office buildings, factories and shopping centres are not taking place at the usual rate. We are faced with a very serious situation.
Our post-secondary education has been built on the basis, as an hon. member pointed out, that 80 per cent of the university educational process is paid for by the state. However, the student or his family still has to pay a substantial university fee to enable him to attend university. The student or his family must find the money. Since 1945, more and more university students have been depending on work with fairly adequate wages for the 41 to 5 months of the year when they are not attending university. Until recently it was relatively easy for most students who wanted to work, to find employment. This matter should be discussed some time in the House or in committee to see whether it is the best way to operate our educational system. Possibly we have passed the time when students should be attending school seven months of the year and away from school the other five months. I do not have the time, and this is not the place, to go into detail. Suggestions were made earlier today about a trimester system. The suggestions have merit.
It is not the fault of the university students if the federal and provincial governments have not worked out alternative systems to the one in practice today. This is something the students have a right to expect because we want them to attend university. If one reads the newspaper, listens to the radio or watches television he is told that if one wants to succeed in this world and obtain the best job, he must have a better education.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
How many times have we heard speeches from the minister and from others-and I have made my share-which have pointed out that the largest percentage of the unemployed comprises those with the least education? We
May 8, 1970

have been encouraging our young people to attend university, technical and vocational schools or community colleges, and implicit in our encouragement was the belief of ourselves and our students that students would be able to find work during the period when school was closed.
As I said earlier, over 600,000 students are now looking for work and I presume another half-million will be looking for work at the end of June. As at last March there were 542,000 people looking for work, and the figure for May is probably higher. So there is not only potential, but real competition for the jobs available between those who want full-time work and university or high school students who want part-time work.
Last year and the year before the Department of Manpower and Immigration conducted a fairly effective drive to find jobs for university students, and I cannot fault them for that. But when one examines the record to see what happened, while nobody actually lied about the success of the program-certainly not the department or the minister-we would be exaggerating if we were to pat ourselves on the back and say we did a successful job.
Let me refer, as I am sure the minister will, to the summer employment survey of postsecondary students in Canada, 1969, prepared by the Department of Manpower and Immigration. Looking at the survey one finds that last year almost 350,000 students were looking for summer work. This figure represents about 90 per cent of those young people who were at high school or university. Looking further, one sees that in Canada as a whole 93 per cent of our students who sought work obtained paid summer work in Canada.
I am sure the minister will use that statistic, or something very similar to it, when he rises to speak. The position was, of course, much worse in Newfoundland where only 79 per cent of the students who were looking for work found paid work; but nevertheless that figure does make the situation look pretty good. At least, it does until one notes the next set of figures in the report, which show that the average time worked by male students was 12 weeks during the summer of 1969, and by female students only 11 weeks. I am not a mathematician, but one does not need to be a mathematician to realize that since most university students have five months away from school, this gives them 20 weeks in which to

Student Summer Employment work. Yet we find the average period worked was 11 weeks for women and 12 weeks for male students.
I	suggest to the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker, that this situation represents a disaster. Our students need work for the whole summer if they are to continue their studies in the coming year without having to bear a debt or to impose a real burden on their families. I am sure that the minister, who himself was a university professor before entering politics full time, knows something about the expense involved in being a student. He knows how much a set of books costs, regardless of the course being taken by the student. He knows something about upkeep costs and about how much money a student, no matter how modest his needs, must have for spending purposes. So that if students can average a work period that amounts to only 60 per cent of their available time, the situation is really disastrous.
I see my time is nearly up, but I want to suggest to the minister, while giving the officials of his department high marks for effort, that the department's efforts are doomed to failure and that the problems facing our students will multiply unless and until the government drops its short-sighted policy of combating inflation by encouraging, in fact by forcing, higher unemployment. The burden of such a program must by the very nature of things fall most heavily on students and part time workers.
I suggest to the minister that instead of a very elaborate and extensive program that is designed to find work for students at a time of substantial unemployment, the minister should direct his very considerable efforts and ability to persuading the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benson) that they are adopting the wrong course by embarking, with the support of the governor of the Bank of Canada, the chairman of the Prices and Incomes Commission and the Deputy Minister of Finance, upon a deliberate policy of creating more unemployment than this country has had for many years. If our unemployment figures continue to spiral they will soon be compared with the very heavy unemployment suffered in the pre-World War
II	depression period.
In light of this situation, the task of finding employment for university and other postsecondary education students is doomed to failure. The government ought to reverse its present policy and instead adopt a policy of full employment. The government should
May 8. 1970

Student Summer Employment expand the economy and meet the needs of our people for housing, recreational services, and so on. This sort of policy would not bring on large-scale student unemployment and we would not need the kind of specialized programs that the department is planning for this year.

speakeroldname: Hon. Allan J. MacEaclien (Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the debate on the motion moved by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) and I thank hon. members for the seriousness with which they have treated the subject of student summer employment. The motion was somewhat broader than the particular problem of student summer employment and could have embraced in its discussion other activities of the department, including our "Operation Retrieval", our student exchange program with other countries and our efforts to find a permanent place for graduates of universities in the Canadian labour market.
Naturally, hon. members have focused their attention on the immediate question now before the House, namely, the problem of providing jobs for the very large number of students who will be coming on to or are presently on the Canadian labour market. I am pleased that once again the opposition has directed the attention of the House to the programs and policies of the Department of Manpower and Immigration.
[DOT] (4:20 p.m.)
It is not surprising that the members of the opposition should refer back again and again to the programs and policies of this department, because we do administer a variety of complex programs which affect very closely the lives of many Canadians. Sometimes I wonder whether people fully realize the extent of our contact with the public in all phases of the department including immigration as well as manpower.
I hope this motion will have the effect of drawing greater support for the programs that are already in effect in Canada to assist students this summer. The motion is a bit too late to have any influence on programs that could be put into effect for this summer. However, in the department over the winter months, beginning last fall, we have been at work preparing a summer program. We have been in contact with a variety of organizations in preparing this summer program. So while we appreciate the somewhat belated [Mr. Orlikow.l
motion on this subject put forward by the opposition, we hope it will have the effect of encouraging the highest possible employment for students this summer.
Mr. Speaker, the problem is clear. There is an increasing number of students entering the labour force for temporary employment as a result of two factors, namely, the increasing youthful population in Canada and the increasing participation of Canadian youth in the educational process. When the schools and universities close in the spring, the students come on to the labour market for temporary employment. They come on to the labour market in order to obtain jobs so that they can earn money with which to continue their education in the fall. This problem, which became acute last summer, may remain acute this summer and will probably become more acute later in the 1970's. This summer there will be a total of 641,000 students on the labour market.
I should like to draw to the attention of the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Orli-kow) that his estimate was highly exaggerated. The estimate in respect of secondary, post-secondary and university students is about 641,000. Of that figure 385,000 are in university now or will be in university in the fall. The remaining group is composed of high school students in secondary institutions down to grade 10. This number is about 256,000. Therefore, it is important to retain that figure in mind, that is, that the number of students who will be going to university and who will be seeking jobs this summer is about 385,000. That is an increase over last year.
In the government's hiring policies we give priority to students who are now in university or who are about to enter university. These students have the first chance at jobs in the government because their need in respect of income obviously is greater. So of the total of 641,000 there is a total of 385,000 students now in or entering university this fall, plus an additional 256,000 students at the secondary school level. This is the problem we must face.
I do not agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North when he says that in the present structural arrangement it is not necessary to have a special program. Unless there is a drastic reorganization in the university and school system, which is within provincial jurisdiction, to assist in this problem we will have this temporary demand on the labour market every summer for a grow*

May 8. 1970
ing number of jobs for students and we will have to have a special program for this special problem.
I should like to say that we should not "knock" the success of last year's student employment program. It was not perfect; we admit that improvements are needed, especially in respect of lengthening the period of employment available to students. But there were pretty encouraging results. The results were much more encouraging than the doleful predictions which had been made by members of the opposition as we entered into the summer period last year. I was greatly worried concerning the performance, or the possible performance of our program last summer.
I was greatly heartened by the result of the survey to which the hon. member for Winnipeg North referred. At least in his judgment it was a fairly effective drive. I think it was better than that.
In order to test the adequacy of our program, very early in the summer-in the spring-we decided to have a survey carried out at the universities and colleges in order to find out from the students what their summer experience had been. My hon. friend has referred to this survey. We have not tried to conceal its results. It has good parts, and there are parts we would like to change. It indicated that 93 per cent of the students in colleges and universities who wanted jobs, obtained jobs last summer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: For part of the summer.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
The survey also indicated the number of students who had jobs for the whole summer, for half the summer and for less than half the summer. There is a major improvement to be made in our performance in the direction of lengthening the work experience of each student. With that I agree with the hon. member for Winnipeg North.
I believe in their speeches this afternoon hon. members have taken a somewhat pessimistic attitude. Perhaps their intention was to urge us on to greater efforts.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext:
It may also have the effect of creating a pessimistic attitude about the labour market for students this summer. The results last summer were pretty good; even the hon. member for Winnipeg North described them as fairly effective. I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) who, when we announced our program in July last summer,
Student Summer Employment took note of our efforts and made a positive statement about the probable results of our program last summer. The positive results did take place; jobs were obtained by 93 per cent of those who sought jobs. The students who were employed last summer earned $300 million. This is rather important; it is not a trivial sum. To suggest that the effort, not only by the federal government but also by the provincial governments, the university associations and the employers, brought about a trivial result I believe is totally inaccurate and damaging to the efforts we are making this summer.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
Ninety-three per cent did get jobs-all for as long as they wanted-and they earned $300 million. We say now that with the difficulties we face in the general labour market, plus the increased number of students-the 10 per cent that are coming out this summer-we are bending our efforts to do as well, and hope to do better this summer. Our program was announced on May 4. Hon. members dismissed it as if it were of no consequence. It is of some consequence. We have put out $250,000 in advertising to draw to the attention of employers in Canada the need of taking on students in order to meet the social issues that have been raised throughout this debate. It is not a question of a job; it is a question of the approach of society as a whole to this particular generation and the evaluation of the contribution it will make to Canada as well as its confidence in the ability of this generation to make a contribution to the productive machinery.
We try to set the pace federally. We are taking on 11,365 students this year. Last year we took on quite a number. Over a two-year period since 1968 we have increased our hirings as an employer by 27 per cent. That is a pretty good record. If employers and provincial governments in Canada would do as well, there would be practically no student summer unemployment problem in Canada in 1970. These students who will work for the federal government this year will earn about $12 million. In my department I am taking on 570 students. About 400 of them will be working in Manpower centres across Canada, helping other students get jobs. Surely if the students are as keen on getting jobs for themselves as we think they are, this body of almost 400 students will have a major impetus to do what we propose to do.
I want to go back for a moment to the results of a survey that was made last sum-
May 8, 1970

Student Summer Employment
mer. The survey showed that 72 per cent of the students founds jobs in private industry, 14 per cent with provincial governments, 7 per cent with the federal government and 7 per cent with municipal administrations. Governments provided close to 30 per cent of the jobs. The rest must come from private industry. It would be foolish on my part to develop a strategy without taking into account the fact that the major contribution to the resolution of this problem must take place within the private sector of the Canadian economy.
I am delighted to tell the House that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce very early this year, not suddenly in May or in April but in December or early this year began to promote its Operation Placement, a student summer employment program. The program is under the chairmanship of Mr. Scrivener, the president of Bell Canada and he and his committee have taken the question of student employment very seriously. They have put out a booklet called "Operation Placement". It is a new effort this summer. In this booklet the problem of student employment is analysed in the way that it has been analysed today and the numbers of students and the importance of solving the problem are studied. They go on to say:
It goes without saying that the Canadian businessman holds the solution to this problem.. .Every effort must be made to find as many productive openings as are economically feasible.
An hon. member touched upon the necessity of meaningful employment. It seems to me to be dangerous to take on students merely for the sake of taking them on without giving them something meaningful and substantial to do. In my own department we take on students for the summer and we are attempting to work out meaningful jobs so that at the end of the summer, even though they will have earned $1,000 or more, they will not have also developed a contempt for an organization that has put them in the system and does not give them anything meaningful to do. What Mr. Scrivener and his committee are saying in this booklet is that these openings must be economically feasible. He goes on to say:
It has been suggested that, since the student labour force in 1970 will amount to approximately 5 per cent of the national labour force, a "5 per cent guideline" be established as a target.
They have gone to their membership and have said that every employer belonging to the Canadian Chamber of Commerce should take on a student-equivalent of 5 per cent of its normal labour force. If the employers in [Mr. MacEachen.l
Canada will do that, as requested by the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, and if employers in Canada will do as the federal government has done, there will be no student employment problem this summer. The key to this problem, no matter how much we can do as governments at the federal, provincial and municipal levels, will depend upon what private employers will do in planning their efforts to take on an increasing number of students.
We know that the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski) is interested in the question of student employment. He has helped in that field in the past. What can Members of Parliament do to help, in addition to making speeches and drawing the attention of the country to this problem? They can do what I hope the hon. member for Edmonton Centre will do, that is call by phone employers throughout the country and throughout their constituencies and ask, "Will you take on 5 per cent? Will you do what the federal government is doing? Will you do what the Canadian Chamber of Commerce recommends?" It would be a very important part of the program now if we got this impetus from Members of Parliament who appreciate the importance of summer student employment.
We have talked about what the government is doing, what we did last year, what we are hoping to do this year and what the Canadian Chamber of Commerce is proposing to do. I want to say a word about a person who has not been mentioned yet, that is, the student himself or herself. We still believe in individual responsibility.

speechtext: They will provide the leadership. Give them a chance.

The most effective person in the job getting field is the student. As we talk about all these programs, let us remember that the boy or girl who gets the job this summer is the boy or girl who goes and digs for the job. I received a letter last week or the week before from a lady in Chilliwack, British Columbia. She had been watching our TV commercials showing a group of students talking about summer employment and saying, "We need work," or words to that
May 8. 1970	COMMONS
effect. She wrote something that I thought was very important:
[DOT] (4:40 p.m.)
As I watch this film I ask myself these questions:
1.	Why aren't they portrayed at least making an attempt to find work for themselves?
2.	What do they appear to have done to equip themselves for summer work?
As a mother of a 17 year old girl who worked hard towards her Royal Lifesaving medals since she was 12, I can tell you she has no trouble getting a summer position. However, she has planned ahead for her high school and university summer vacations.
The average employer is looking for young people able to sell themselves, because they in turn will be able to sell his merchandise or services.
I quote those paragraphs merely to underline to hon. members that the underpinning of our program is the quality of the student, the way he puts himself forward and the efforts he will make to get a job this summer. I firmly believe that a sincere attempt by students will get a sincere response from most employers.
The hon. member for South Western Nova (Mr. Comeau) made a pretty good speech. The only parts I did not like were sections which I thought I heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) deliver a year or so ago on the same subject, but the rest of it was pretty good.

speechtext:
I have no complaint, but 1 regret that anyone would describe the speech as containing anything other than research from former editions of Hansard. But that is sometimes a pretty good place to go. The hon. member asked for a national conference on employment. Well, Mr. Speaker, the National Employment Committee met yesterday in Ottawa. Where are these bright research boys who are not watching what is happening?
Our National Employment Committee met yesterday. It is working effectively in order to bring together what is required to have a successful program this summer. My department was represented along with the Association of College Placements, the Economic Council of Canada and the Canadian Chamber of Commerce. They reviewed our common program, including the government, business and the universities. There has been a good response, for example in the advertising field. I am quoting from a rough report from this meeting but I think it might give hon. members a sense of what is happening in this country. First, with respect to advertising
DEBATES	6773
Student Summer Employment they say that in addition to the promotion gained from our $260,000 campaign it was reported that the Financial Post had devised a letter encouraging student employment and a reprint of our major newspaper advertisement was sent by it to 13,000 subscribers and businessmen across Canada. That is one effort-a small effort, but a very important one.
The representative of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce reported that their program, Operation Placement, has been put into motion and that at least 160 Operation Placement committees have been established by the Chamber across Canada, all working closely with Canada Manpower centres. Some 60 of these are in the province of Quebec, but all the committees are located in major communities and student density areas. The representative of the Canadian Chamber of Commerce pointed out that the intention of the federal government to employ so many students this summer has been of great help in their program when approaching employers across Canada.
I do not want for a moment to underestimate the nature of the problem or the importance of solving it this summer. I hope we will be able to do as well this year as we did last year. Co-operation will be required. Cooperation has already come from business and industry. I hope it will be forthcoming from hon. gentlemen opposite and from hon. gentlemen on this side of the House, many of whom are active in areas where the hiring of students comes within their purview.
It has been pointed out that this is a serious matter for students. While there are loans and bursaries, all students are not able to avail themselves of these avenues of financing education. Indeed, while some students have access to loans and bursaries they would much prefer to graduate without any financial obligations and enter life without that additional encumbrance. We give them credit for that. The problem of financing their education is a serious and important one. We have taken action to give jobs in the government. Private industry is taking action to assist in getting jobs as well. We know that as a government we cannot solve the problem alone. We cannot solve the problem of poverty alone. It involves the active co-operation of the private sector.
I should also point out that there are students who may not want to take jobs this summer. The world is changing. Travel is becoming more popular. Affluence is apparent

May 8, 1970

Student Summer Employment for some students. This is not just a poverty-stricken class totally. For example, last summer some students wanted to become better acquainted with the world in which we live and 14,000 of them went travelling. I am glad that there is that kind of opportunity. When I was a student, the thought of going travelling for the summer was out of the question. But according to our survey 14,000 Canadian students last summer were able to put the question of work out of their minds and go travelling.
Some 5,000 students did voluntary work. For one reason or another they were in a position to take on voluntary work. Another group of about 24,000, either because they had to catch up on courses or because they wanted to accelerate their education, stayed on at university. There is a whole spectrum to the problem. It is a very dynamic process. There is an interaction between the community and the employers and the world, and the world does not impinge as much upon the Canadian student as it does upon the rest of us.
The comment that the government does not care, cannot be taken seriously. We are proud of our young generation. We are proud of the students of Canada. We are not as young as we used to be, but we still appreciate the idealism and the sensitivity of young people. Certainly this government wants to maintain its links with the young generation and wants to maintain a sensitive approach, not basically for political purposes but because, as has been pointed out in the debate, the very survival of our country and of our institutions depends upon the confidence that the young people of Canada have in these institutions.
As one person, one member and one minister, I have great confidence in the youth of Canada. I am grateful that they are not embroiled in the difficulties in which, unhappily, the youth of the United States find themselves.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-LACK OF STUDENT EMPLOYMENT OPPORTUNITIES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know there is a great deal of mobility in the student population, but we do not have a special program for helping students to move. From my knowledge of the labour market I know that students from the Atlantic provinces, for example, travel all over Canada to take jobs in the course of the summer, and that is a very good thing.
